> One of the bedrock tenets of democracy is that if you put something up for a vote the you have to accept the results of that vote. Sure, but that just means the way referenda are done should be better thought out in general. It's not a matter of that one specifically, it's just a fact of life that the percentage of the population that supports something will drift significantly over time, and the way we sample that support is noisy enough that the results would likely change by several percentage points if you held two consecutive votes on two consecutive days, nevermind leaving a few months between them. This means that when using a referendum to decide on something which is impossible, or at least extremely costly, to undo later, a single vote at one point in time coming out to 50.000001% is simply inadequate. At an absolute bare minimum, there should be several votes over an extended period of time, say 5 over 1 year, and whichever option wins more of the votes is ultimately selected (vote can end early if there is no possibility of victory for the other choice any longer, and I guess you could have a "result over 70% for either side instantly seals it" kind of rule too) Something even better would involve properly modeling voter sentiment over time through a number of votes and meticulous Bayesian inference on the results, with a pre-specified confidence threshold before a result can be called either way. But I know some people are philosophically opposed to "overly complicated" electoral systems because of reasons (that I disagree with, but that's going wildly off-topic, so I'll leave it at that), so I could leave with the simpler system, even if it is still flawed and prone to "erroneous" results in edge cases. Still, it'd be infinitely better than a "hurr durr 50.000001% result for ritual suicide of the whole nation, the people have spoken there is nothing that can be done".
